course.title: Human Resource Management
course.description: How organizations find, grow, reward, and retain the people who do the work — from strategic HR and hiring to development, performance, pay, and employee relations. Structure adapted from OpenStax Human Resource Management (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: Human resource management is best described as…
options: the strategic management of an organization's people
questions.explanation: HRM is the strategic management of people — recruiting, developing, rewarding, and retaining talent to meet business goals.

questions.prompt: 'Strategic HR' means HR should mainly…
options: align people practices with business strategy
questions.explanation: Strategic HR ties workforce decisions to what the business is trying to achieve — see 'What HR does'.

questions.prompt: A structured, job-related process for choosing among applicants is called…
questions.explanation: Selection is the process of evaluating candidates against job requirements.

questions.prompt: Onboarding is best defined as…
options: helping a new hire become effective and connected
questions.explanation: Onboarding integrates new hires so they reach productivity faster — see 'Onboarding & development'.

questions.prompt: A performance review that only happens once a year and surprises the employee usually fails because…
options: feedback should be frequent and have no surprises
questions.explanation: Good performance management gives ongoing feedback, so the review confirms rather than surprises.

questions.prompt: Total compensation includes…
options: base pay plus benefits and other rewards
questions.explanation: Total compensation combines base pay, variable pay, and benefits.

questions.prompt: Which is a core reason equal-employment law matters in hiring?
options: it prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics
questions.explanation: Anti-discrimination law protects candidates from bias based on protected characteristics.

questions.prompt: Employee engagement most directly refers to…
options: employees' emotional commitment to their work and organization
the size of the HR team
questions.explanation: Engagement is discretionary effort driven by commitment — it predicts retention and performance.

lessons.title: What HR does — and why it's strategic
lessons.grammar_note: 'People' is the work; 'strategy' is the why. HR links the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the main functions of HR and what makes HR *strategic*. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, why is 'align people practices with business strategy' a better definition than 'hiring and firing'?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: HR covers a connected cycle: *workforce planning* (what talent do we need?), *recruitment and selection* (finding and choosing people), *onboarding and development* (helping them grow), *performance management* (setting expectations and feedback), *compensation and benefits* (rewarding them fairly), and *employee relations* (a fair, engaged, lawful workplace). HR becomes *strategic* when these choices are driven by business goals — not done as isolated paperwork. If a company's strategy is fast growth, HR builds pipelines and scalable onboarding; if it's quality and retention, HR invests in development and engagement.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A software firm plans to double its engineers in a year. Strategic HR asks: what skills, from where, at what cost, and how do we keep them? It builds a hiring pipeline, a 30-day onboarding plan, and a pay band benchmarked to the market — instead of reacting to each resignation one at a time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each activity to its HR function: (1) writing a job description, (2) running a new-hire's first week, (3) benchmarking salaries to the market, (4) planning how many roles you'll need next quarter, (5) handling a harassment complaint. Answers: 1-recruitment/selection, 2-onboarding, 3-compensation, 4-workforce planning, 5-employee relations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating HR as only administrative. Mistake: thinking 'strategic' means cutting people. Exit: (a) Name three of HR's functions. (b) What makes HR strategic rather than administrative? Answers: any of planning/recruiting/onboarding/performance/compensation/relations; aligning people decisions with business strategy.

lessons.title: Recruitment and selection
lessons.grammar_note: Recruit = attract a pool; select = choose from it. Different jobs.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish recruitment from selection and choose fair, job-related selection methods. Warm-up: which comes first, building a candidate pool or evaluating candidates?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Recruitment* attracts a qualified pool of applicants — through job postings, referrals, and sourcing. *Selection* evaluates that pool to predict who will succeed. Good selection starts from a *job analysis*: the real duties and requirements of the role. From those you build *job-related criteria* and consistent methods — *structured interviews* (same questions, same rubric for everyone), *work samples*, and *reference checks*. Consistency and job-relevance make selection both more accurate and more fair, and they reduce the risk of bias against protected groups.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Hiring a support agent, a team writes three scenarios (an angry customer, a refund edge case, a bug report) and scores every candidate on the same 1–5 rubric. An unstructured 'tell me about yourself' chat would have rewarded whoever felt familiar; the structured work sample rewards who can actually do the job.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as recruitment or selection: (1) posting a role on a job board, (2) scoring a coding exercise, (3) asking employees for referrals, (4) checking references, (5) sourcing candidates on LinkedIn, (6) a structured panel interview. Answers: 1-recruitment, 2-selection, 3-recruitment, 4-selection, 5-recruitment, 6-selection.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging 'culture fit' by gut feel — it smuggles in bias; use job-related criteria instead. Mistake: asking each candidate different questions. Exit: (a) What does a job analysis give you? (b) Why are structured interviews fairer? Answers: the real duties and requirements to build criteria from; every candidate is judged on the same job-related questions and rubric.

lessons.title: Onboarding, training, and development
lessons.grammar_note: Onboarding starts people; development keeps growing them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how onboarding, training, and development differ and why each pays off. Warm-up: what should a new hire be able to do by the end of week one versus month three?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Onboarding* is the structured process that turns a new hire into an effective, connected team member — logistics, role clarity, early wins, and relationships. *Training* builds the specific skills the current job needs. *Development* is longer-term growth for future roles and responsibilities. A common frame is the *70-20-10* idea: most growth comes from challenging work (70), some from others and feedback (20), and some from formal courses (10). Investment here shows up as faster time-to-productivity and lower early turnover.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A new analyst's onboarding sets a 30-60-90 plan: by day 30 they run a standard report unaided (training), by day 60 they own a recurring dashboard, by day 90 they propose one improvement (development). Each milestone is observable, so both sides know whether it's working.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as onboarding, training, or development: (1) a first-week buddy and setup checklist, (2) a course on the team's analytics tool, (3) stretch-leading a small project to prepare for a lead role, (4) explaining the mission and who's who on day one, (5) coaching toward a future management path. Answers: 1-onboarding, 2-training, 3-development, 4-onboarding, 5-development.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating onboarding as one HR orientation day, then leaving the manager to wing it. Mistake: confusing training (this job) with development (next job). Exit: (a) What is the goal of onboarding? (b) In 70-20-10, where does most learning happen? Answers: make the new hire effective and connected quickly; from challenging on-the-job work.

questions.prompt: HR is 'strategic' primarily when it…
options: aligns people practices with business strategy
questions.explanation: Strategic HR links workforce decisions to business goals.

questions.prompt: Recruitment differs from selection because recruitment…
questions.explanation: Recruitment attracts; selection chooses.

questions.prompt: The foundation of fair, job-related selection criteria is a…
questions.explanation: Job analysis defines the real duties and requirements.

questions.prompt: Structured interviews improve fairness mainly because…
options: every candidate gets the same questions and rubric
questions.explanation: Consistency reduces bias and improves accuracy.

questions.prompt: Onboarding's goal is to…
options: make a new hire effective and connected quickly
questions.explanation: Onboarding speeds time-to-productivity and belonging.

questions.prompt: In the 70-20-10 model, most development comes from…
questions.explanation: The '70' is learning by doing challenging work.

lessons.title: Performance management and feedback
lessons.grammar_note: Performance management is a year-round loop, not a once-a-year form.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the performance-management cycle and give feedback that's specific and fair. Warm-up: why is a manager who saves all feedback for the annual review setting the employee up to fail?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Performance management is a continuous loop: *set clear goals* (often SMART — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), *give ongoing feedback*, *coach*, and *review* against the goals that were set. Good feedback is *specific* (about behavior and impact, not personality), *timely* (close to the event), and *actionable* (the person knows what to do next). The annual review should hold no surprises, because the feedback happened all year. Rating everyone must rest on job performance, applied consistently, to stay fair and defensible.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Weak: 'You're not a team player.' Strong: 'In yesterday's launch, the release notes went out without QA sign-off, which delayed two customers. Next time, please confirm sign-off in the checklist before publishing.' The strong version names the behavior, the impact, and the fix — so it can actually change what happens next.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Rewrite or judge each: (1) 'Great job lately' — is it specific? (2) Turn 'be more proactive' into a specific ask. (3) 'You always mess up' — what's wrong with it? (4) Is 'your report was 2 days late twice this month; let's plan deadlines together' good feedback? Answers: 1-no, it's vague; 2-e.g. 'flag risks in the Monday standup before I ask'; 3-it attacks the person and uses 'always'; 4-yes, specific, timely, and actionable.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: recency bias — judging a whole year by the last two weeks. Mistake: feedback aimed at personality ('you're lazy') instead of behavior. Exit: (a) Name two traits of good feedback. (b) Why should an annual review hold no surprises? Answers: any two of specific/timely/actionable; because feedback was given continuously all year.

lessons.title: Compensation and benefits
lessons.grammar_note: Total rewards = base pay + variable pay + benefits (+ the intangibles).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Break total compensation into its parts and explain internal versus external equity. Warm-up: is base salary the whole of what an employer 'pays' someone?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Total compensation* has parts: *base pay* (fixed salary or wage), *variable pay* (bonuses, commission, incentives tied to results), and *benefits* (health coverage, retirement contributions, paid leave). Employers aim for two kinds of fairness: *internal equity* (people in comparable roles are paid comparably inside the company) and *external equity* (pay is competitive with the market, set using *salary benchmarking*). *Pay transparency* and consistent structures help defend against pay-discrimination claims and build trust. Benefits often drive retention as much as headline salary.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Two candidates get 'the same offer' of $70,000 base. But one role adds a 10% target bonus, full health premiums, and a 5% retirement match; the other has none. The *total compensation* differs by well over $10,000 a year even though the base looks identical — which is why offers should be compared as total rewards.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as base pay, variable pay, or a benefit: (1) monthly salary, (2) sales commission, (3) health insurance, (4) annual performance bonus, (5) paid vacation, (6) retirement match. Answers: 1-base, 2-variable, 3-benefit, 4-variable, 5-benefit, 6-benefit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: comparing only base salary between offers. Mistake: confusing internal equity (fair inside the firm) with external equity (competitive vs the market). Exit: (a) Name the three parts of total compensation. (b) What is salary benchmarking for? Answers: base pay, variable pay, benefits; setting pay competitively against the external market.

lessons.title: Applied project: design a hiring and onboarding plan

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one real role you understand (e.g. a customer-support agent, a junior developer, or a barista). Design a fair, job-related plan to hire someone into it and get them productive. You won't run it — you'll plan it rigorously and ethically.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Write a short job analysis: 4-6 real duties and the must-have requirements. 2) Recruitment: name two sources you'd use to build a candidate pool. 3) Selection: choose two job-related methods (e.g. a structured interview and a work sample) and one job-related criterion each is scored on — every candidate assessed the same way. 4) Onboarding: a 30-60-90 plan with one observable milestone per stage. 5) Fairness check: name one thing you'll do to reduce bias and stay within equal-employment principles.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Duties and requirements are specific and clearly tied to the job. ✔ Selection methods are job-related and applied consistently to every candidate (not gut-feel 'fit'). ✔ Onboarding milestones are observable, so you'd know if they were met. ✔ Your fairness step actually reduces bias (e.g. same rubric for all, structured questions, criteria set before meeting candidates). If all four hold, you've designed like an HR professional.
